exam: A 12‑year‑old boy presents with rapid height gain and enlarged hands. What is the next best investigation? — IGF‑1 level to confirm GH excess; if high, proceed to MRI pituitary.
A patient with gigantism is started on octreotide but develops gallstones. What is the mechanism? — Somatostatin analogues reduce gallbladder motility, predisposing to stones.
A child with tall stature has normal IGF‑1 but GH fails to suppress on OGTT. What does this suggest? — GH‑secreting pituitary adenoma.
Which complication is most likely to cause early death in untreated gigantism? — Cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure.
A patient with gigantism has normal growth plates but shows facial coarsening. What is the diagnosis? — Acromegaly (GH excess after epiphyseal closure).
What is the first‑line medical therapy for GH‑secreting adenoma? — Somatostatin analogue (octreotide).
ai.title: Gigantism
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Gigantism is excess growth hormone before epiphyseal closure, causing abnormal linear growth. It is usually due to a GH‑secreting pituitary adenoma. Early recognition and treatment prevent irreversible complications.

sections.p: Gigantism is a rare endocrine disorder characterised by excessive linear growth in children and adolescents due to chronic excess of growth hormone (GH) before the growth plates fuse. The most common cause is a pituitary adenoma, but other causes exist.

b: GH binds GH receptor → JAK2/STAT5 pathway → IGF‑1 production
IGF‑1 acts on growth plates and cartilage
sections.p: GH stimulates liver production of insulin‑like growth factor‑1 (IGF‑1), which promotes bone and soft tissue growth. In gigantism, unregulated GH secretion keeps the growth plates open, leading to tall stature.
Normal GH secretion is pulsatile and suppressed by somatostatin, stimulated by GHRH, and feedback inhibited by IGF‑1. In a GH‑secreting adenoma, this regulation is lost.

b: Excess GH → high IGF‑1 → bone overgrowth
GH excess after epiphyseal closure → acromegaly
sections.p: Uncontrolled GH leads to excessive longitudinal bone growth, soft tissue swelling, and metabolic disturbances. Early epiphyseal closure can paradoxically cause short stature later.

b: Height >97th percentile for age and sex
sections.p: Patients present with rapid height gain, macrocephaly, enlarged hands/feet, and early puberty. Untreated, they develop hypertension, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and osteoarthritis.

t.b: Elevated IGF‑1 confirms GH excess; normal range 100–300 ng/mL depending on age

t.a: GH suppression test (oral glucose tolerance test)
t.b: Failure to suppress GH (<1 µg/L) indicates GH‑secreting adenoma
Localises adenoma; size >6 mm suggests clinical significance

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, focus on clinical features and basic labs. If available, use IGF‑1 and MRI; otherwise, rely on growth velocity and physical exam.

t.b: Increase >2 cm/year in a child >5 years suggests GH excess
Elevated levels support diagnosis; normalisation after treatment indicates response
Identifies adenoma; absence does not exclude disease if GH/IGF‑1 are high

b: Somatostatin analogue reduces GH and IGF‑1
sections.p: Treat the underlying adenoma first. Somatostatin analogues (octreotide) are first‑line; surgery is definitive. Monitor for cardiovascular and metabolic complications.

t.b: Reduces GH secretion; monitor for gallstones and glucose intolerance
Adjunct if residual tumour or recurrence

b: Acromegaly: enlarged hands/feet but normal height
sections.p: Acromegaly (GH excess after epiphyseal closure), pituitary gigantism due to other hormones, and constitutional tallness.
IGF‑1 can be low in malnutrition or liver disease; GH suppression test can be falsely normal if performed incorrectly.
Remember the sequence: rapid height gain → macrocephaly → enlarged hands/feet → hypertension. Key investigations are IGF‑1 and GH suppression test.

t.a: What is the diagnostic criterion for GH excess?
t.b: IGF‑1 above age‑adjusted upper limit AND failure to suppress GH <1 µg/L on OGTT

t.a: Why is octreotide preferred over dopamine agonists?
t.b: Octreotide directly inhibits GH; dopamine agonists are less effective for GH adenomas

t.a: Can a child with gigantism develop early puberty?
t.b: Yes, GH excess can accelerate puberty; monitor pubertal staging

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid height gain >2 cm/year in a child >5 years
Hypertension or cardiomegaly in a tall child
Diabetes mellitus onset in a child with tall stature
